title: Idioms & Phrases
summary: One idiom per shift, four meanings, and the literal option always planted as bait. Idioms are frozen pictures — animals, body parts, colours, food — and every bank below decodes them into families so that even a half-remembered idiom yields its meaning. 130+ idioms with meanings written for daily 15-minute banking.

subtopics.title: Why literal meaning is always wrong — and how to find the picture
subtopics.concept: An idiom is a fixed group of words whose meaning is not the meaning of the separate words. The words paint a picture, and the meaning is what the picture stands for. The exam always plants a literal option, so cross it out first.

tricks.title: Photo test
tricks.body: If you could take a photo of what an option says, it is almost always wrong. This removes one option in nearly every question.

example.q: Break the ice: (a) to crack frozen water (b) to start a conversation among strangers (c) to feel cold (d) to make a drink
steps: Crack frozen water and make a drink are pictures.
Start a conversation is the figurative meaning.
example.answer: (b) to start a conversation among strangers

tricks.title: Plug-back check
tricks.body: Put your chosen meaning into a sentence in place of the idiom. If the sentence sounds natural, keep it.

tricks.title: Tone from the key word
tricks.body: Cold, dark and hot often signal trouble. Cloud nine and red-letter signal joy. Use this when you do not know an idiom.

mistakes.wrong: Choosing the option that repeats the words of the idiom.
mistakes.right: Cross out any option you could photograph. It is a literal decoy.

mistakes.wrong: Learning an idiom by its words but not its picture.
mistakes.right: Learn the picture and what it stands for.

mistakes.wrong: Ignoring the tone of the idiom.
mistakes.right: Say if it is happy, sad or angry. Pick the same tone.

mistakes.wrong: Matching on one shared word (beans, milk).
mistakes.right: Look-alike idioms share a word but not a meaning. Learn them in pairs.

mistakes.wrong: Skipping the sentence in a context question.
mistakes.right: Let the situation in the sentence fix the meaning.

subtopics.notes:
### What an idiom is
An **idiom** is a group of words with a meaning that is different from its single words.

*He let the cat out of the bag.* This has nothing to do with a cat or a bag. It means he told a secret by mistake.

The words paint a picture. The idiom means what that picture stands for.

### How wrong options are built
An idiom question gives one idiom and four meanings. The wrong options come in three kinds.
1. **The literal option.** It repeats the actual words: *smell a rat* becomes "to smell a dead rat".
2. **The neighbour option.** A figurative meaning that sounds close but is not right: *turn a deaf ear* becomes "to hear badly".
3. **The opposite or random option.** It has the reverse sense or belongs to another idiom.

Only one option gives the accepted meaning.

### The four-step method
1. **Kill the literal.** If you could take a photo of what the option says, it is almost always wrong. *Break the ice* does not mean to crack frozen water.
2. **Find the picture.** A cat escapes from a bag. Something hidden comes out. So a secret is revealed.
3. **Check the tone.** Is the idiom happy, sad, angry or neutral? *In hot water* means trouble, not danger of death.
4. **Plug it back.** Put the option into a small sentence. *The plan ended in smoke* becomes *the plan came to nothing*. That sounds right.

> **Rule:** If an option can be pictured physically, cross it out first.

### Idioms that look alike
Many idioms share a word but mean different things. Examiners put one twin in the options for the other.
| Idiom | Meaning | Look-alike | Its meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| spill the beans | tell a secret | cry over spilt milk | waste regret on what cannot be undone |
| once in a blue moon | very rarely | a bolt from the blue | a sudden shock |
| smell a rat | suspect a trick | the rat race | a tiring fight for success |
| in a nutshell | in brief | in a pickle | in a difficult situation |

> **Tip:** Learn each pair together on one card. Then the planted twin cannot fool you.

### Idiom inside a sentence
Sometimes the idiom sits in a sentence. Use the sentence as a clue.

*Meena was on cloud nine after the result.* The result is good news. So the meaning is extremely happy.

### When you do not know the idiom
- Remove the literal options first.
- Judge the tone from the key word. Cold, dark and hot often mean trouble. Cloud nine and red-letter mean joy.
- Choose the option that fits a sentence you can imagine.

> **Watch:** Two figurative options can look alike. Pick the one that names the outcome the idiom records. Bite the dust means be defeated, not be wounded.

patterns.name: Idiom with a literal decoy
patterns.howToSpot: One idiom stands alone under 'select the most appropriate meaning'. At least one option repeats its words.
steps: Cross out every option you could photograph.
Ask what picture the idiom paints.
Say what the picture stands for.
patterns.why: The literal option is always planted as bait.

example.q: Let the cat out of the bag: (a) to free a pet (b) to reveal a secret (c) to buy a bag (d) to hide a pet
steps: Free a pet and hide a pet are literal.
A cat escaping means something hidden comes out.

patterns.name: Idiom inside a sentence
patterns.howToSpot: A full sentence holds the idiom, often in bold, and you choose its meaning there.
steps: Decide if the situation is good or bad.
Remove options with the wrong tone.
patterns.why: The situation fixes the tone.

example.q: Meena was on cloud nine after the result. (a) extremely happy (b) flying (c) confused (d) ill
steps: Flying is literal. Confused and ill are wrong in tone.

patterns.name: Close figurative trap
patterns.howToSpot: Two options are figurative. One is the real meaning. The other sounds related but changes the sense or strength.
steps: Ask what result the idiom records.
Pick the one that states that result.
patterns.why: The neighbour option is the most common trap after the literal one.

example.q: Bite the dust: (a) be wounded (b) be defeated (c) clean a floor (d) be tired
steps: Wounded and tired are related but not the record of the idiom.
Bite the dust means be defeated.

patterns.name: Look-alike idiom pairs
patterns.howToSpot: The options include the meaning of another idiom that shares a key word: beans and milk, blue moon and blue bolt.
steps: Name the twin idiom in the options.
patterns.why: Twin idioms are planted for readers who match on one word.

example.q: Spill the beans: (a) regret what cannot be changed (b) tell a secret (c) waste food (d) cook a meal
steps: Option (a) is the meaning of cry over spilt milk.
Waste food and cook a meal are literal.
Spill the beans means tell a secret.

patterns.name: Tone check
patterns.howToSpot: The options differ in strength: suspect, be sure, be certain.
steps: Mark the idiom as mild, strong or neutral.
Match the strength of each option.
patterns.why: A right idea in the wrong strength is still wrong.

example.q: Smell a rat: (a) to suspect that something is wrong (b) to be certain of theft (c) to smell something rotten (d) to feel ill
steps: Suspect is at the right strength.
example.answer: (a) to suspect that something is wrong

revision: An idiom is a fixed picture. The meaning is what the picture stands for.
Wrong options: literal, neighbour, opposite.
Method: kill the literal, find the picture, check the tone, plug back.
Learn look-alike idioms in pairs.
In a sentence, the situation decides the meaning.

subtopics.title: Animal and body-part idioms
subtopics.concept: Many exam idioms use an animal or a body part. Each animal has a fixed character and each body part a fixed job. Use that to work out an idiom even when you half remember it.

tricks.title: Character first
tricks.body: Name the animal or body part, then recall its character or job. The meaning usually follows.

example.q: Keep the wolf from the door: (a) to scare a wolf (b) to earn enough to avoid hunger (c) to close a door (d) to be a wolf
steps: Scare a wolf and close a door are literal.
The meaning is to earn enough to avoid hunger.
example.answer: (b) to earn enough to avoid hunger

tricks.title: Body parts in sets
tricks.body: Learn hand idioms together: lend a hand, have your hands full, wash your hands of. The job is help or work.

tricks.title: One card for opaque idioms
tricks.body: Write a card for each idiom whose picture is hard to see. Read those cards first in revision.

mistakes.wrong: Reading pull someone's leg as hurting someone.
mistakes.right: It means to tease playfully.

mistakes.wrong: Reading cold shoulder as an illness.
mistakes.right: It means to treat someone coldly.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing smell a rat with the rat race.
mistakes.right: Smell a rat means suspect a trick. The rat race is a tiring fight for success.

mistakes.wrong: Reading heart in your mouth as love.
mistakes.right: It means extreme fear or nervousness.

mistakes.wrong: Reading wash your hands of as cleanliness.
mistakes.right: It means to refuse any more responsibility.

subtopics.notes:
### Why animals and body parts
Many idioms in exams name an **animal** or a **part of the body**. Each one has a fixed character. So you can often decode an idiom even if you only half remember it.

### Animal characters
| Animal | Stands for | Idiom | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| bull | facing force head-on | take the bull by the horns | face a problem boldly |
| rat | cheating, trickery | smell a rat | suspect something is wrong |
| crocodile | false tears | crocodile tears | pretended sorrow |
| horse | speed, hurry | hold your horses | wait, be patient |
| wolf | hunger | keep the wolf from the door | avoid hunger |
| birds | targets | kill two birds with one stone | get two results from one action |
| lion | biggest share | the lion's share | the largest part |
| goose | foolish effort | a wild-goose chase | a pointless search |
| cat | hidden thing | let the cat out of the bag | reveal a secret |

> **Example:** Crocodile tears. The old belief was that crocodiles cry while eating. So the tears are not real. The meaning is pretended sorrow.

### Body-part jobs
| Part | Job | Idiom | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| ear | listening | turn a deaf ear | refuse to listen |
| eye | watching, agreeing | see eye to eye | agree fully |
| nose | price paid | pay through the nose | pay far too much |
| shoulder | welcome | give the cold shoulder | treat someone coldly |
| neck | risk | stick your neck out | take a risk by acting boldly |
| feet | courage | get cold feet | lose courage at the last moment |
| hand | help, work | lend a hand | give help |
| hands | work | have your hands full | be very busy |
| foot | firmness | put your foot down | take a firm stand |
| heart | fear, feeling | heart in your mouth | very nervous |
| leg | play | pull someone's leg | tease playfully |

### More body idioms
- *Bite the dust*: be defeated or fail completely.
- *Bury the hatchet*: end a quarrel and make peace.
- *Wash your hands of*: refuse any more responsibility.
- *Keep at arm's length*: avoid becoming friendly with.
- *Cost an arm and a leg*: be extremely expensive.
- *Keep an eye on*: watch carefully.

### Four question types
1. **Animal idiom.** Use the animal's character.
2. **Body idiom.** Use the body part's job.
3. **Idiom in a sentence.** The sentence tells you if it is good or bad.
4. **Reverse type.** A meaning is given and you choose the idiom. The wrong options are real idioms of the same body part. Match the job exactly. Hand is help, hands full is busy, wash hands is refuse duty.

> **Watch:** Some idioms have no clear picture. Keep one flash card each for cold shoulder, bite the dust and crocodile tears.

patterns.name: Animal idiom meaning
patterns.howToSpot: The idiom names an animal or bird: bull, rat, crocodile, wolf, horse, goose, lion.
steps: Match the character to an option.
patterns.why: Each animal keeps the same character in every idiom.

example.q: Take the bull by the horns: (a) to face a difficulty boldly (b) to buy a bull (c) to run away (d) to lose a bet
steps: The bull stands for facing force head-on.
So it means to face a difficulty boldly.

patterns.name: Body-part idiom meaning
patterns.howToSpot: The idiom names a body part: ear, eye, nose, shoulder, neck, feet, hand, heart.
steps: Match the job to an option.
patterns.why: Each body part has a job that carries into the idiom.

example.q: Turn a deaf ear: (a) to hear badly (b) to refuse to listen (c) to listen carefully (d) to be ill
steps: Hear badly is the neighbour trap.
Deaf ear means refusing to listen.

patterns.name: Animal or body idiom in a sentence
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence holds the idiom, and you choose its meaning in context.
steps: Decide if the situation is good or bad.
Use the animal or body job.
patterns.why: The sentence confirms the character.

example.q: He stuck his neck out for his friend. (a) took a risk (b) hurt himself (c) ran away (d) told a lie
steps: The action helps a friend, so the tone is bold.

patterns.name: Choose the idiom for a meaning
patterns.howToSpot: The stem gives a meaning and the options are four idioms, usually of one body part.
steps: Say the meaning in two words.
Match each idiom to its meaning.
Pick the one that fits exactly.
patterns.why: The wrong options are real idioms with other meanings.

example.q: Which idiom means to be extremely busy? (a) lend a hand (b) have one's hands full (c) wash one's hands of (d) keep at arm's length
steps: Wash hands is refuse duty and arm's length is avoid friendship.

patterns.name: Playful or hostile trap
patterns.howToSpot: An option gives a harmful meaning for a mild idiom (pull someone's leg, give the cold shoulder).
steps: Mark the idiom as mild or hostile.
Cross out options with the wrong strength.
patterns.why: Body idioms are often milder or colder than the literal picture.

example.q: Pull someone's leg: (a) to hurt someone (b) to tease someone playfully (c) to help someone walk (d) to trip someone
steps: Hurt, help walk and trip are literal.

revision: Animal is character: bull bold, rat trick, crocodile fake, wolf hunger, horse hurry.
Body is job: ear listen, eye watch or agree, neck risk, feet courage, hand help.
Reverse questions: match the meaning to the body part's job first.
Keep separate cards for cold shoulder and crocodile tears.
Hands full is busy. Wash hands is refuse duty.

subtopics.title: Colour and food idioms
subtopics.concept: In English idioms each colour carries a feeling, and food is used to judge a task or a person. Learn the colour or food and you know the family of the meaning. Watch the look-alike pairs, such as red tape and red-letter day.

tricks.title: Colour to feeling
tricks.body: Say the colour and its feeling before you read the options. Blue means sudden or rare, and the options then sort themselves.

example.q: Out of the blue: (a) completely unexpectedly (b) very sadly (c) after a long wait (d) at sea

tricks.title: Food gives a verdict
tricks.body: Ask what verdict the food gives: easy, hard, flattery or trouble. That is the meaning.

tricks.title: Pair cards
tricks.body: Write the twins on one card: red tape and red-letter day, apple of the eye and apple of discord.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing red tape with a red-letter day.
mistakes.right: Red tape is delay. A red-letter day is a happy day.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing the apple of one's eye with the apple of discord.
mistakes.right: The first is most loved. The second is a cause of a quarrel.

mistakes.wrong: Reading a food idiom literally (a piece of cake as a treat).
mistakes.right: Food idioms judge a task or a person. Cake means easy.

mistakes.wrong: Filling a blank without checking the grammar.
mistakes.right: After was, choose a noun phrase such as a red-letter day.

mistakes.wrong: Learning colours without their feelings.
mistakes.right: Learn the feeling: blue unexpected, green envy, black disgrace.

subtopics.notes:
### Colours carry feelings
Each colour usually points to one family of meaning.
| Colour | Usual meaning | Idiom | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| blue | unexpected, rare | out of the blue | suddenly, without warning |
| blue | unexpected, rare | once in a blue moon | very rarely |
| red | anger | see red | become suddenly angry |
| red | officialdom | red tape | too many official rules causing delay |
| red | special day | a red-letter day | a day to remember |
| green | envy | green with envy | very jealous |
| black | disgrace | a black sheep | the one who brings shame to a group |
| white | costly, useless | a white elephant | costly to keep and of no use |
| grey | unclear | a grey area | a matter not clearly right or wrong |
| silver | wealth | born with a silver spoon | born into a rich family |

> **Example:** A flyover that nobody uses but costs lakhs to maintain is a white elephant. It is a possession that costs much and gives no benefit.

### Watch out for red
Red has three families.
- *See red* means to become angry.
- *Red tape* means too many official rules causing delay.
- *Red-letter day* means a happy, important day. Special days were marked in red on calendars.

Examiners put these three against each other.

### Food idioms are judgements
A food idiom uses something we eat to judge a task or a person.
| Idiom | Judgement | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| a piece of cake | easy | a very easy task |
| a hard nut to crack | difficult | a difficult problem or person |
| butter someone up | flattery | praise someone to get a favour |
| food for thought | thinking | something worth thinking about |
| a hot potato | controversy | an issue everyone avoids handling |
| in a pickle | trouble | in a difficult situation |
| the apple of one's eye | love | the person loved most |
| spill the beans | secret | reveal a secret |
| the salt of the earth | goodness | a very good, dependable person |
| carry coals to Newcastle | useless supply | take something to a place that has plenty |
| a storm in a teacup | fuss | a big quarrel over a small matter |

> **Example:** Maths is a piece of cake for Arjun. Cake means easy, so maths is very easy for him.

### Look-alike pairs
- *The apple of one's eye* (most loved) and *the apple of discord* (cause of a quarrel).
- *A piece of cake* (easy) and *a hot potato* (a touchy issue).
- *Red tape* (delay) and *red-letter day* (a happy day).
- *Born with a silver spoon* (rich from birth) and *every cloud has a silver lining* (some good in every bad situation).

### Blank-filling questions
A sentence has a blank and four idioms as options.
1. Decide what the sentence needs: a useless thing, a small fuss, a happy day.
2. Pick the idiom of that family.
3. Check the grammar. A blank after *was* needs a noun phrase such as *a red-letter day*.

patterns.name: Colour idiom meaning
patterns.howToSpot: The idiom holds a colour word: blue, red, green, black, white, grey, silver.
steps: Match the feeling to an option.
patterns.why: A colour keeps one feeling across many idioms.

example.q: Once in a blue moon: (a) very rarely (b) at night (c) very often (d) in a hurry
steps: Blue stands for rare or unexpected.

patterns.name: Food idiom meaning
patterns.howToSpot: The idiom names a food: cake, nut, butter, potato, pickle, beans, milk, apple, salt.
patterns.why: Food idioms judge a task or a person.

example.q: A piece of cake: (a) a birthday treat (b) a task needing almost no effort (c) a costly gift (d) a sweet dish
steps: Birthday treat and sweet dish are literal.
The meaning is a task needing almost no effort.
example.answer: (b) a task needing almost no effort

patterns.name: Look-alike twin
patterns.howToSpot: One option is the meaning of a twin idiom that shares the colour or food word.
patterns.why: The twin is planted for readers who match only the colour.

example.q: Red tape: (a) a happy day (b) excessive official delay (c) sudden anger (d) a costly item
steps: A happy day is red-letter day.
Red tape is excessive official delay.

patterns.name: Fill the blank with an idiom
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence has a blank and four idioms as options.
steps: Pick the idiom of that family.
patterns.why: The sentence names the need before the options do.

example.q: The flyover that nobody uses but costs lakhs to maintain is a ___. (a) white elephant (b) black sheep (c) red-letter day (d) hot potato
steps: The sentence describes something costly and useless.
Black sheep is a person and red-letter day is a happy day.

patterns.name: Choose the idiom for a meaning
patterns.howToSpot: The stem gives a meaning and the options are four idioms of one colour or food family.
steps: Say the meaning in two words.
Match each idiom to its meaning.
patterns.why: The wrong options are real idioms with other meanings.

example.q: A person who brings shame to his family: (a) black sheep (b) white elephant (c) dark horse (d) grey area
steps: White elephant is a costly useless thing.

revision: Blue is sudden or rare. Red is anger, delay or a special day. Green is envy. Black is shame. White is costly and useless. Grey is unclear.
Food is judgement: cake easy, nut hard, butter flattery, potato touchy, pickle trouble, apple loved.
Learn look-alike pairs together.
In blanks, decide the need first, then the family, then check grammar.

subtopics.title: Idioms for situations and types of people
subtopics.concept: Many idioms describe situations, such as trouble, effort or suddenness, and types of people, such as false, weak or reliable. Sort each idiom into a family and the right option stands out. A few idioms come from old stories, and one line of the story gives the meaning.

tricks.title: Family first
tricks.body: Name the family of the situation before you read the options. Effort, trouble and suddenness cover a large share.

example.q: At the drop of a hat: (a) instantly (b) carefully (c) slowly (d) angrily
steps: The idiom is in the sudden family.
Carefully and slowly are the opposite.

tricks.title: One line per story
tricks.body: Store each story idiom as one line: Achilles, heel, weak point. Do not learn the whole story.

tricks.title: Read the whole sentence
tricks.body: In a blank question, say what the person does. Escape means took to his heels. Hard work means burnt the midnight oil.

mistakes.wrong: Reading pass the buck as passing money.
mistakes.right: It means to shift blame or duty to someone else.

mistakes.wrong: Reading steal a march on as stealing.
mistakes.right: It means to gain an advantage over someone.

mistakes.wrong: Reading under the weather as being in the rain.
mistakes.right: It means slightly ill.

mistakes.wrong: Reading play second fiddle as music.
mistakes.right: It means to accept a lower role.

mistakes.wrong: Guessing a story idiom without the story.
mistakes.right: Recall the one-line story and turn it into a meaning.

subtopics.notes:
### Two big groups
1. **Situation idioms** describe what is happening: trouble, hard work, sudden events, success, defeat.
2. **People idioms** describe a type of person: loyal, false, weak, skilled.

Find the group and the family. Then the answer stands out.

### Situation families
| Family | Idioms | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Trouble | in hot water | in serious trouble |
| Hard effort | burn the midnight oil | work late into the night |
| Hard effort | leave no stone unturned | try every possible means |
| Hard effort | move heaven and earth | make the greatest effort |
| Sudden | at the drop of a hat | instantly |
| Sudden | on the spur of the moment | without planning |
| Sudden | a bolt from the blue | a sudden shock |
| Money | make both ends meet | live within a small income |
| Change | turn over a new leaf | begin a better way of living |
| Change | turn the tables | reverse the position |
| Winning | carry the day | win |
| Losing | throw in the towel | admit defeat and give up |
| Losing | take to one's heels | run away quickly |
| Mood, health | on cloud nine | extremely happy |
| Mood, health | under the weather | slightly ill |

> **Example:** The police left no stone unturned to find the child. This is the effort family. The meaning is tried every possible way.

### More situation idioms
- *A blessing in disguise*: a misfortune that turns out well.
- *Out of the frying pan into the fire*: from a bad situation into a worse one.
- *Face the music*: accept the unpleasant results of one's acts.
- *Pass the buck*: shift blame or duty to someone else.
- *End in smoke*: come to nothing.
- *Against all odds*: despite every difficulty.
- *In the doldrums*: low in spirits or activity.

### People families
| Type | Idiom | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| False friend | a snake in the grass | a treacherous enemy hiding as a friend |
| False friend | a fair-weather friend | a friend only in good days |
| False friend | a wolf in sheep's clothing | a dangerous person who looks harmless |
| Weak | a man of straw | a person of no substance |
| Weak | a cog in the machine | an unimportant worker in a big system |
| Reliable | a man of his word | one who keeps his promises |
| Reliable | a tower of strength | a person who gives firm support |
| Many skills | a jack of all trades | does many jobs, masters none |
| Second place | play second fiddle | accept a lower role |

### Idioms from stories
One line of the old story fixes the meaning.
- **Achilles' heel**: a Greek hero could be hurt only at his heel. It means a weak point.
- **Bell the cat**: the mice wanted a bell on the cat, but none dared tie it. It means take a big risk for everyone.
- **Pandora's box**: opening a forbidden box let out all troubles. It means a source of many problems.
- **A Herculean task**: Hercules did twelve very hard labours. It means a task needing huge effort.
- **Midas touch**: whatever King Midas touched became gold. It means the ability to make money from anything.
- **A Trojan horse**: soldiers hid inside a wooden horse. It means something harmless-looking that harms from inside.

> **Watch:** *Pass the buck* is not about money. *Steal a march on* is not stealing. *Under the weather* is not about rain.

patterns.name: Situation idiom meaning
patterns.howToSpot: The idiom describes an event or condition: trouble, effort, suddenness, winning, losing, health.
steps: Recall the meaning of that family.
patterns.why: One family word tells you the answer.

example.q: Leave no stone unturned: (a) to try every possible means (b) to clean the ground (c) to give up early (d) to break stones
steps: Clean the ground and break stones are literal.
Give up early is the opposite.
The idiom is in the effort family.

patterns.name: People idiom meaning
patterns.howToSpot: The idiom names a type of person: a ___ friend, a man of ___, a ___ in the grass.
steps: Name the type: false, weak or reliable.
Recall the idiom in that type.
patterns.why: People idioms come in fixed types.

example.q: A snake in the grass: (a) a lazy person (b) a treacherous enemy hiding as a friend (c) a snake catcher (d) a loyal helper
steps: A snake hides and strikes, so it is a treacherous enemy.
example.answer: (b) a treacherous enemy hiding as a friend

patterns.name: Fill the blank with a situation idiom
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence has a blank and four idioms as options.
steps: Pick the idiom of that family.
patterns.why: The sentence shows the family before the options do.

example.q: Seeing the police, the thief ___. (a) took to his heels (b) burnt the midnight oil (c) turned over a new leaf (d) played second fiddle

patterns.name: Idioms from stories
patterns.howToSpot: A name or story object appears: Achilles, Pandora, Hercules, Midas, Trojan, a cat with a bell.
steps: Recall the story in one line.
Turn the story into a meaning.
patterns.why: The story line fixes the meaning.

example.q: Achilles' heel: (a) a sore foot (b) a weak point (c) a great strength (d) a fast runner
steps: The hero could be hurt only at his heel.
So it means a weak point.

patterns.name: Bad to worse and blame idioms
patterns.howToSpot: The idiom describes a change in a situation or a shift of blame.
steps: Name the situation: worse, blame or result.
patterns.why: These idioms record an outcome, not an action.

example.q: Out of the frying pan into the fire: (a) from a bad situation into a worse one (b) from cooking to eating (c) from cold to warm (d) from work to rest
steps: Frying pan is bad and fire is worse.
So it means from bad to worse.
example.answer: (a) from a bad situation into a worse one

revision: Name the family first: trouble, effort, sudden, money, change, win, lose, health.
False people: snake in the grass, fair-weather friend, wolf in sheep's clothing.
Weak people: man of straw, cog in the machine. Reliable: man of his word, tower of strength.
Story idioms: Achilles' heel, bell the cat, Pandora's box, Herculean, Midas touch, Trojan horse.
In blanks, match the family the sentence needs.

subtopics.title: Phrasal verbs (verb + particle phrases)
subtopics.concept: A phrasal verb is a verb joined with a small word called a particle, such as up, off, out or in. Together they give a new meaning, like give up, which means stop. They appear in idiom questions, fill-in-the-blank and error spotting.

tricks.title: Swap for one word
tricks.body: Replace the phrasal verb with one plain word, such as cancel, refuse or tolerate. Test it in the sentence.

example.q: The meeting was put off. It was: (a) postponed (b) cancelled forever (c) held early (d) put out
steps: Cancelled forever and held early do not fit.

tricks.title: Subject shows the particle
tricks.body: A car breaks down. A fire breaks out. A thief breaks in. The subject picks the particle.

tricks.title: Learn by verb
tricks.body: Learn one verb with all its particles in one sitting: give up, give in, give away, give out.

mistakes.wrong: Guessing a phrasal verb from the verb alone.
mistakes.right: The particle changes the meaning. Learn the whole phrase.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing put off and put out.
mistakes.right: Put off means postpone. Put out means extinguish.

mistakes.wrong: Writing 'run out sugar'.
mistakes.right: Write 'run out of sugar'. Keep both particles.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing break down, break out and break in.
mistakes.right: Down means stop working. Out means start suddenly. In means enter by force.

mistakes.wrong: Learning particles as strict rules.
mistakes.right: They are tendencies. Learn each common phrase with its meaning.

subtopics.notes:
### What a phrasal verb is
A **phrasal verb** is a verb plus a small word called a **particle**. The particle can be up, off, out, in, on, down, after, into or over.

Together they give a new meaning that you often cannot guess from the verb alone.
- *give* means hand over. *give up* means stop doing something.
- *call* means phone or shout. *call off* means cancel.

Exams test them as a meaning question, a blank to fill with a particle, or a word to replace.

### What the particles usually mean
These are tendencies, not strict rules. They still help.
| Particle | Usual idea | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| off | stop, cancel, leave | call off (cancel), put off (postpone), take off (leave the ground) |
| out | finish, remove, appear | run out of (finish), put out (extinguish), break out (start suddenly) |
| up | complete, stop, arrive | give up (stop), turn up (arrive), bring up (raise a child) |
| down | reduce, fail, refuse | break down (stop working), turn down (refuse), look down upon (despise) |
| in | enter, yield | give in (surrender), hand in (submit), break in (enter by force) |
| after | follow, care | look after (take care of), take after (resemble an elder) |
| into | examine, meet | look into (investigate), run into (meet by chance) |
| over | recover, check | get over (recover from), look over (check quickly) |

### One verb, many meanings
Examiners fix the verb and change the particle.
| Verb | Particle | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| give | up, in, away, out | stop a habit, surrender, donate or reveal, distribute |
| turn | down, up, out | refuse, arrive, prove to be |
| take | after, off, up | resemble, leave the ground, start a hobby |
| break | down, out, in, up | stop working, start suddenly, enter by force, end a relationship |
| come | across, about | meet by chance, happen |
| put | off, out, up with | postpone, extinguish, tolerate |

> **Example:** The car broke ___ on the highway. Cars stop working, so the answer is *broke down*. *Broke out* is for war, fire or disease. *Broke in* is for thieves.

### Three-word phrasal verbs
Some phrasal verbs have two particles. They must stay together.
- *put up with*: tolerate.
- *run out of*: have none left.
- *look down upon*: despise.
- *look forward to*: wait eagerly.

> **Watch:** Do not drop the second particle. "We have run out sugar" is wrong. Say "run out **of** sugar".

### How to answer
1. **Meaning questions.** Replace the phrasal verb with one word, such as cancel or tolerate, and test it in a sentence.
2. **Particle blanks.** Read the whole sentence. The subject (a car, a fire, a meeting) shows which particle fits.
3. **Replace-the-word questions.** The bold word is formal, such as extinguish or postpone. Find the phrasal verb that means the same.

patterns.name: Meaning of a phrasal verb
patterns.howToSpot: A phrase such as 'to call off' or 'to put up with' is given. The options are short meanings.
steps: Split the verb and the particle.
Try each option in a sentence.
patterns.why: The particle carries the new meaning.

example.q: To call off: (a) to cancel (b) to phone (c) to shout (d) to visit
steps: Phone and shout are the meanings of call alone.

patterns.name: Fill in the particle
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence has a blank right after a verb. The options are particles.
steps: Name the subject: a car, a fire, a meeting.
Pick the particle that fits that subject.
patterns.why: The subject shows which meaning is needed.

example.q: The car broke ___ on the highway. (a) in (b) out (c) down (d) off
steps: Break in is for thieves and break out is for war or fire.

patterns.name: Same verb, different particles
patterns.howToSpot: All options share one verb: give up, give in, give away, give out.
steps: Say the meaning in one word.
Match each option to its meaning.
patterns.why: Only the particle changes the meaning.

example.q: The rebels finally ___ and laid down their weapons. (a) gave up (b) gave in (c) gave away (d) gave out
steps: Give away means donate and give out means distribute.

patterns.name: Replace a formal word
patterns.howToSpot: A sentence has a formal verb in bold (extinguish, postpone, recover). The options are phrasal verbs.
steps: Say the formal word in plain words.
Match a phrasal verb to it.
patterns.why: A phrasal verb is the everyday form of a formal word.

example.q: The firemen quickly EXTINGUISHED the fire. (a) put off (b) put out (c) put up (d) put down

patterns.name: Three-word phrasal verb
patterns.howToSpot: The blank sits after a two-part verb such as run out ___ or look forward ___.
steps: Do not drop the second particle.
Pick the particle that completes it.
patterns.why: These phrases are fixed.

example.q: We have run out ___ sugar. (a) from (b) of (c) off (d) with
steps: The phrase is run out of.

revision: off is cancel or stop. out is finish or remove. up is stop or arrive. down is refuse or fail. after is care or resemble. into is investigate.
call off cancel, put off postpone, put out extinguish, put up with tolerate.
give up stop, give in surrender, turn down refuse, take after resemble.
break down stops working, break out starts suddenly, come across meets by chance, get over recovers.
Keep three-word phrases whole: run out of, look forward to.

subtopics.title: Exam strategy: banking 300 idioms in 30 days
subtopics.concept: Idioms are a small but steady part of the English section. The pool is small and repeats often, so a bank of about 300 idioms covers most papers. Learn in a 30-day plan and use your own sentences.

tricks.title: Own sentence
tricks.body: Write one sentence of your own for each idiom. The sentence is what you remember under pressure.

tricks.title: Format first
tricks.body: Name the format before you start. Meaning, replace, complete or opposite. Each has its own first step.

tricks.title: Same-meaning trap
tricks.body: In an opposite question, the option with the same meaning as the idiom is always wrong.

example.q: Opposite of A TOWER OF STRENGTH: (a) a strong supporter (b) an unreliable person (c) a tall building (d) a man of his word
steps: A tower of strength gives firm support.
Strong supporter and man of his word mean the same.
An unreliable person is the opposite.

mistakes.wrong: Reading a list of idioms once.
mistakes.right: Write one sentence of your own for each idiom.

mistakes.wrong: Accepting a changed word in an idiom.
mistakes.right: Idioms are frozen. Learn the exact words.

mistakes.wrong: Choosing the same meaning in an opposite question.
mistakes.right: Write the meaning first, then reverse it.

mistakes.wrong: Learning idioms in alphabet order.
mistakes.right: Learn by family so the clusters help recall.

mistakes.wrong: Spending too long on one unknown idiom.
mistakes.right: Judge the tone, pick an option and move on.

subtopics.notes:
### How idioms appear
Idioms give a small but steady number of marks. Most papers ask one or two direct idiom questions. Idioms also hide inside cloze tests, sentence improvement and fill-in-the-blank items.

The pool of idioms that examiners use is small and repeats often. A list of about 300 idioms covers most of what you will see.

### Question formats
1. **Meaning of the idiom.** One idiom, four meanings. The most common.
2. **Replace the phrase.** A plain phrase is underlined, and you choose the idiom that can replace it. *They are in bitter open hostility* becomes *they are at daggers drawn*.
3. **Complete the idiom.** One word is missing: *calls a spade a ___*. Only the original word is correct.
4. **Opposite meaning.** Find the meaning first, then its opposite.
5. **Idiom inside a passage.** The context gives the tone.

### Idioms are frozen
You cannot change the words of an idiom. It is *a hard nut to crack*, never *a hard nut to break*. It is *every cloud has a silver lining*, never *a golden lining*.

That is why a complete-the-idiom question has only one defensible answer. When you learn an idiom, learn its exact words.

### The 30-day plan
| Days | Daily work |
|---|---|
| 1 to 10 | 10 new idioms, one sentence of your own for each |
| 11 to 20 | 10 new and 15 old, revised by family |
| 21 to 30 | 10 new, 25 old and one 20-question self-test |

Any idiom you miss twice goes on a short **weak list**. Revise that list once a week.

> **Tip:** Your own sentence is what you remember in the exam. A list read alone fades fast. Example: I burnt the midnight oil before my mock test.

### In the exam hall
About 20 seconds per idiom.
1. Kill the literal option.
2. Find the picture and the family.
3. Check the tone: positive or negative.
4. Plug the answer back into a sentence.

If you do not know the idiom, judge the tone from the key words. Pick the option with the same tone. This beats a blind guess.

### Sorting idioms by family
Group idioms so that one cue recalls many.
- **Effort:** burn the midnight oil, leave no stone unturned, move heaven and earth.
- **Trouble:** in hot water, in a pickle, out of the frying pan into the fire.
- **Secrets:** spill the beans, let the cat out of the bag.
- **Defeat:** bite the dust, throw in the towel.

When two idioms in a question sit in one family, compare their exact meanings.

### After each mock test
List every idiom you missed. Write its meaning and one sentence of your own. Read the list again after two days and after a week.

> **Note:** Ten idioms known well are worth more than fifty half known.

### Opposite-meaning questions
Write the meaning in two words first. *Keep one's chin up* means stay cheerful. So the opposite is lose heart.

> **Watch:** The option that says "stay brave" has the same meaning. It is the planted trap.

patterns.name: Complete the idiom
patterns.howToSpot: An idiom has one word blanked, and the options are four close words (spade, shovel, tool).
patterns.why: Idioms are frozen, so only the original word is correct.

example.q: He always calls a spade a ___. (a) shovel (b) spade (c) tool (d) digger
steps: The idiom is call a spade a spade.
Only the original word is correct.

patterns.name: Replace the phrase with an idiom
patterns.howToSpot: A plain phrase is underlined and the options are idioms.
steps: Say the meaning of the phrase in two words.
Match each idiom to a meaning.
patterns.why: The answer is the idiom with exactly that meaning.

example.q: They are in bitter open hostility. (a) at daggers drawn (b) on cloud nine (c) in the doldrums (d) under the weather
steps: The meaning is open and bitter enmity.
Cloud nine is joy and doldrums is low spirits.

patterns.name: Idiom from any family with a tone check
patterns.howToSpot: A less known idiom appears and the options differ in tone.
steps: Judge the tone from the key word.
Pick the option with the same tone.
patterns.why: Tone alone beats a blind guess.

example.q: In the doldrums: (a) in high spirits (b) low in spirits or activity (c) in great danger (d) in a hurry

patterns.name: Opposite in meaning to an idiom
patterns.howToSpot: The stem asks for the option opposite in meaning to the idiom.
steps: Write the meaning of the idiom in two words.
Cross out the option that has the same meaning.
patterns.why: The option with the same meaning is the planted trap.

example.q: Opposite of KEEP ONE'S CHIN UP: (a) stay brave (b) lose heart (c) work hard (d) speak plainly
steps: Keep one's chin up means stay cheerful.
Stay brave has the same meaning.

patterns.name: Frozen wording in a proverb
patterns.howToSpot: A well-known saying has one word blanked or changed in the options.
steps: Recall the saying word for word.
Find the option with the original word.
patterns.why: A changed word makes a wrong idiom.

example.q: Every cloud has a silver ___. (a) lining (b) edge (c) coat (d) spoon
steps: The saying is every cloud has a silver lining.
It means some good in every bad situation.

revision: 10 new idioms a day, one sentence each, a weekly weak list.
Idioms are frozen. Never accept a changed word.
Formats: meaning, replace the phrase, complete the idiom, opposite, in a passage.
Exam steps: kill the literal, find the picture, check the tone, plug back.
Opposite question: meaning first, then reverse. Cross out the same-meaning option.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: One idiom is given on its own and you must choose its meaning from four options. At least one option simply repeats the idiom's words.
pyqPatterns.approach: Cross out every literal option first. Then ask what the picture in the idiom stands for and choose that meaning. Put your answer back into a short sentence to check that it reads naturally.

example.q: Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom: *To throw in the towel*
example.solution: A towel thrown into a boxing ring stops the fight → **to admit defeat and give up**. 'Clean up after a game' is the literal decoy.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The idiom is printed in bold inside a sentence, and the options are possible meanings.
pyqPatterns.approach: Decide from the sentence whether the situation is good or bad news. Remove options with the wrong tone, then test the survivors in place of the idiom.

example.q: *The minister's promise **ended in smoke**.* Meaning?
example.solution: A promise that ends in smoke disappears → **came to nothing**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The idiom contains an animal (bull, rat, crocodile, wolf) or a body part (ear, eye, neck, feet, hand).
pyqPatterns.approach: Use the animal's fixed character (crocodile = fake, bull = bold) or the body part's job (ear = listen, neck = risk). This decodes most such idioms even if you only half remember them.

example.q: Meaning of *Crocodile tears*

pyqPatterns.pattern: Colour and food idioms, including look-alike twins
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A colour (red, blue, green, white, black) or a food (cake, nut, potato, apple) appears in the idiom; often one option is the meaning of a twin idiom.
pyqPatterns.approach: Recall the colour's feeling or the food's judgement. Watch the three reds: see red (angry), red tape (official delay), red-letter day (happy day). Cross out the twin idiom's meaning.

example.q: Meaning of *Red tape*
example.solution: **Too many official rules causing delay**. 'A memorable day' is the twin (red-letter day).

pyqPatterns.pattern: Fill in the blank with an idiom
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A sentence has a blank and the four options are idioms.
pyqPatterns.approach: Name what the sentence needs (running away, a lower role, a small fuss, a joyful day). Choose the idiom from that family and read the sentence again to check grammar.

example.q: *Seeing the police, the pickpocket ___.* (took to his heels / broke the ice / kept his chin up / turned a deaf ear)
example.solution: The thief escapes → **took to his heels**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A name or story object appears: Achilles, Pandora, Hercules, Midas, a Trojan horse, belling the cat.
pyqPatterns.approach: Recall the one-line story and turn its key point into a general meaning. Options that retell the story literally are wrong.

example.q: Meaning of *Achilles' heel*
example.solution: The hero could be wounded only at his heel → **a weak point in a strong person or system**.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Replace the phrase with an idiom
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Words in a sentence are in bold; the options are idioms that might replace them.
pyqPatterns.approach: Restate the bold words in two or three plain words, then pick the idiom that has exactly that meaning. The other options are real idioms with different meanings.

example.q: *The workers **were dismissed from their jobs**.*

pyqPatterns.pattern: Complete the idiom / opposite of an idiom
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Either one word of a fixed idiom is missing, or the stem asks for the option opposite in meaning.
pyqPatterns.approach: Idioms are frozen, so only the original word completes them (a spade a **spade**). For opposites, write the meaning first, then reverse it; the option that repeats the meaning is the trap.

example.q: Opposite of *To keep one's chin up*
example.solution: Meaning = stay cheerful; opposite = **to lose heart**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A verb with a particle (call off, put up with, give up) is asked for meaning, or a blank follows a verb and the options are up/off/out/down/in.
pyqPatterns.approach: Use the particle's idea: off = cancel/stop, out = finish/remove, down = refuse/fail, after = care/resemble, into = investigate. Test each option in the sentence.

example.q: *Our car broke ___ on the highway.*

solvedExamples.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To smell a rat
options: to suspect that something wrong is happening
to suffer from a foul smell
solvedExamples.solution: The picture: a rat hiding somewhere, betrayed by its smell — something hidden and dishonest. Hence **to suspect wrongdoing**. The literal options (foul smell, rodents, dead animal) die on the photograph test, and each can be photographed.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Kill what you can photograph; translate the picture: hidden rat = hidden wrongdoing.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A blessing in disguise
options: a misfortune that turns out to be beneficial
a blessing said in a low voice
solvedExamples.solution: The picture: a blessing that arrived wearing the *disguise* of trouble. The abstract meaning: an apparent misfortune that proves beneficial. Options about gifts, costumes or whispers are literal translations of 'disguise' and die at once.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Split the idiom: blessing = good outcome, in disguise = looked bad first.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To pass the buck
options: to shift responsibility to someone else
solvedExamples.solution: From card-playing: the 'buck' (a marker) showed whose turn to deal; passing it handed the duty to another. Hence **shifting one's responsibility to someone else**. Money and betting options trade on the word 'pass' — both are decoys built on the surface vocabulary.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Allusion anchor: the buck = the marker of responsibility; passing it = escaping duty.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Once in a blue moon
practice.solution: A blue moon (a second full moon in a month) hardly ever occurs → **very rarely**. 'Every month' and 'on a full-moon night' are literal moon options — photographable decoys.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To burn the midnight oil
options: to light lamps for a festival
to set something on fire at night
to work or study late into the night
practice.solution: Before electricity, lamps burned oil; burning it at midnight meant **working late**. The image survives as an idiom for late effort.
practice.shortcut: Picture: oil lamp at midnight → late-night work.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A white elephant
practice.solution: Kings once gifted white elephants whose upkeep ruined the receiver — grand to own, ruinous to keep → **a costly, useless possession**. The sacred/rare options take the colour literally.
practice.shortcut: Upkeep test: does keeping it drain you? That is the white elephant.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To beat about the bush
options: to search carefully in a forest
to avoid coming to the point
practice.solution: Hunters beat *around* bushes to flush game without striking it — skirting the centre. Hence **avoiding the main topic**.
practice.shortcut: Picture: striking the edges, never the centre → dodging the point.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To bite the bullet
options: to endure a painful situation bravely
practice.solution: Soldiers once bit a bullet during surgery without anaesthesia — **to bear pain with courage**. 'To give up easily' inverts the meaning; the rest are literal.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To turn a deaf ear
practice.solution: The ear that 'turns away' refuses to hear — **deliberate ignoring**, not physical deafness ('hearing loss' is the literal decoy).
practice.shortcut: Body-function logic: ear = listening; turned away = refusing to listen.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

In hot water
practice.solution: Trouble scalds; being 'in hot water' = **in difficulty or disfavour**. Bath, anger and weather options are temperature-literal.
practice.shortcut: Water temperature = trouble scale: hot water = trouble.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To make both ends meet
practice.solution: One's two 'ends' — income and expense — must touch: **to manage on a limited income**. Ropes, tasks and friendships are literal decoys for 'ends'.
practice.shortcut: Ends = income and expense; making them meet = balancing a budget.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Achilles' heel
options: a weak point despite overall strength
practice.solution: The hero Achilles was invulnerable except where his mother held him — his heel. Hence **the one weakness in a strong person or system**.
practice.shortcut: Allusion anchor: the great hero's single vulnerable spot.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To spill the beans
practice.solution: An upturned jar of beans cannot be taken back — the secret is out → **reveal a secret**. Note the sibling idiom 'cry over spilt milk' (vain regret); papers plant one as the other's decoy.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To pull someone's leg
practice.solution: A playful tug at the leg = **to joke at someone's expense**. The tone is friendly — 'to cheat' and 'to injure' overshoot the idiom's mildness.
practice.shortcut: Tone check: the act is a joke, not an attack.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

At the drop of a hat
practice.solution: A dropped hat was the instant signal to begin a fight or race → **immediately, without needing any reason**. 'Reluctance' and 'planning' contradict the idiom's whole point.
practice.shortcut: Signal picture: hat drops, action starts.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To keep the wolf from the door
options: to guard a house at night
to shut the door in anger
practice.solution: The wolf at the door is hunger; keeping it out means **earning barely enough to live**. House-guarding and pet options are literal.
practice.shortcut: Wolf = hunger; keeping it away = basic survival income.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To smell a rat
practice.solution: A hidden rat betrayed by its smell = a hidden deceit betrayed by signs → **to suspect trickery**. 'To detect a thief red-handed' overshoots — smelling a rat is suspicion, not proof.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To hit the nail on the head
options: to state exactly the right thing
practice.solution: One clean, accurate blow — a description or answer perfectly on target → **to speak with exact correctness**.
practice.shortcut: Accuracy picture: the blow lands precisely.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To break the ice
options: to start a conversation among people who feel shy or stiff
to melt ice for drinking water
practice.solution: *Break the ice* = to get people talking and relaxed in a new or awkward group. 'Melt ice' is the literal decoy; the other two have nothing to do with the picture.
practice.shortcut: Ice = stiffness between strangers; breaking it = starting talk.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To throw in the towel
options: to clean up after a game
to admit defeat and give up
practice.solution: In boxing, a towel thrown into the ring stops the fight. So *throw in the towel* = **admit defeat and give up**. The cleaning and clothes options are literal.
practice.shortcut: Towel thrown → fight stops → give up.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To face the music
options: to accept the unpleasant results of one's own actions
practice.solution: *Face the music* = to accept criticism or punishment for what one has done. The concert and loud-music options are literal; 'run away from punishment' is the opposite.
practice.shortcut: Kill the two music options; the opposite is the last trap.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom in bold.

After failing twice, Ravi decided to **turn over a new leaf** and study every day.
options: to start reading a new book
to start behaving in a better way
practice.solution: The sentence shows Ravi changing his habits after failure. *Turn over a new leaf* = **start a better way of behaving**. Book, tree and school options take 'leaf' literally or guess.
practice.shortcut: Leaf = page of life; a new page = a fresh, better start.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom in bold.

The minister's promise of free laptops **ended in smoke**.
practice.solution: *End in smoke* = to come to nothing after much talk or effort. 'Caused a fire' is literal; 'kept on time' is the opposite.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom in bold.

Meena was **on cloud nine** when she cleared the exam.
practice.solution: Clearing an exam is good news, so the meaning must be positive. *On cloud nine* = **extremely happy**.
practice.shortcut: Good-news sentence → pick the only happy option.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To bury the hatchet
options: to hide a weapon in the ground
to make peace after a quarrel
practice.solution: A hatchet (small axe) stands for the fight; burying it ends the fight. So *bury the hatchet* = **make peace**. 'Keep a secret' borrows the idea of burying but not the fight; 'start a quarrel' is the reverse.
practice.shortcut: Weapon put away for ever = peace.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To get cold feet
options: to catch a cold in winter
to become too nervous to do something one had planned
practice.solution: *Get cold feet* = to lose courage just before doing something planned (a speech, a wedding, a jump). Laziness and loneliness are different feelings; the cold option is literal.
practice.shortcut: Feet = courage to step forward; cold feet = courage fails.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To sit on the fence
options: to avoid taking sides in a dispute
practice.solution: A fence divides two fields; sitting on it means not stepping into either. *Sit on the fence* = **avoid taking sides**.
practice.shortcut: On the fence = in neither camp.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To cry over spilt milk
options: to regret something that cannot be undone
practice.solution: *Cry over spilt milk* = to feel useless regret about what is already done. 'Reveal a secret' is the meaning of its look-alike *spill the beans* — the planted twin.
practice.shortcut: Spilt MILK = regret; spill the BEANS = secret.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A bolt from the blue
options: a sudden and completely unexpected event
practice.solution: *A bolt from the blue* = a shock that comes without any warning (like lightning from a clear sky). 'Very rarely' is the meaning of the twin *once in a blue moon*.
practice.shortcut: BOLT = sudden shock; blue MOON = rare.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

The rat race
options: a tiring and endless struggle for success in modern life
to suspect that something is wrong
practice.solution: *The rat race* = the endless competition for money and position, especially in city jobs. 'Suspect that something is wrong' belongs to the twin *smell a rat*.
practice.shortcut: Rat RACE = competition; SMELL a rat = suspicion.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To take the bull by the horns
options: to face a difficult situation boldly
practice.solution: Grabbing a charging bull by its horns means facing the danger directly. Meaning: **deal with a difficulty boldly**. 'Run away' is the opposite; 'tame an animal' is literal.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Crocodile tears
options: the tears of a wild animal
practice.solution: Crocodiles were believed to shed tears while eating their prey, so the tears were false. *Crocodile tears* = **pretended sorrow**. 'Deep grief' is the opposite (real sorrow).

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To kill two birds with one stone
options: to make two mistakes at once
to achieve two aims with a single action
practice.solution: One stone, two results. Meaning: **get two things done with one effort**. Example: going to the bank on the way to office.
practice.shortcut: Birds = targets; one stone = one action.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To give someone the cold shoulder
options: to treat someone in a deliberately unfriendly way
to push someone away with force
practice.solution: Shoulder = welcome; a cold one = an unfriendly welcome. Meaning: **to ignore or treat someone coldly on purpose**. 'Firm support' confuses it with *a shoulder to lean on*.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To pay through the nose
options: to pay one's bills on time
to pay far more than the fair price
practice.solution: *Pay through the nose* = to be charged much too much. Example: buying water at an airport. The breathing option is literal.
practice.shortcut: Nose idiom about money = paying too much.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom in bold.

The two brothers never **see eye to eye** on money matters.
practice.solution: *See eye to eye* = to agree fully. 'Never see eye to eye' = they always disagree about money. 'Look at each other' is literal.
practice.shortcut: Eye to eye = same view = agreement.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom in bold.

When the boss asked who would take charge of the failing project, only Anil **stuck his neck out**.
options: took a risk by coming forward boldly
practice.solution: Neck = risk. *Stick one's neck out* = to take a risk by saying or doing something bold. Anil volunteered for a risky job.
practice.shortcut: Neck out = exposed to danger = risk.

practice.q: Select the idiom that means *to be extremely busy*.
practice.solution: *Have one's hands full* = be very busy. *Lend a hand* = help; *wash one's hands of* = refuse further responsibility; *try one's hand at* = attempt something new.
practice.shortcut: Full hands = no free hand = busy.

practice.q: Select the idiom that means *to refuse to take any further responsibility for something*.
practice.solution: *Wash one's hands of* a matter = declare you are no longer responsible for it. *Put one's foot down* = take a firm stand; *keep at arm's length* = avoid closeness; *follow in someone's footsteps* = do as an elder did.
practice.shortcut: Washing hands = removing oneself from the matter.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A black sheep
options: a member who brings disgrace to the family or group
the youngest child in a family
practice.solution: Black = disgrace. *A black sheep* is the member whose conduct shames the family or group.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Green with envy
options: new to a job and inexperienced
practice.solution: Green = envy, so *green with envy* = **very jealous**. 'Inexperienced' is a different use of green (a greenhorn), not this idiom.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To see red
practice.solution: Red = anger here. *See red* = to lose one's temper suddenly. 'Notice danger' treats red as a signal light.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A piece of cake
practice.solution: Cake = easy. *A piece of cake* = a task that needs almost no effort.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A hard nut to crack
options: a difficult problem or a person hard to deal with
practice.solution: Nut = hard to open. *A hard nut to crack* = a problem that is difficult to solve or a person who is difficult to handle.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To butter someone up
options: to flatter someone to win a favour
practice.solution: Butter makes things smooth. *Butter someone up* = to praise someone too much so that they will do you a favour.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Red tape
options: too many official rules that cause delay
a ribbon cut at an opening ceremony
practice.solution: Government files were once tied with red tape, and getting them moved was slow. *Red tape* = **official delay caused by rules**. 'A day worth remembering' is the twin *red-letter day*; the ribbon is literal.
practice.shortcut: Red TAPE = delay; red-LETTER day = happy day.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

The apple of one's eye
options: a person who is loved most
practice.solution: *The apple of one's eye* = the person someone loves and cherishes most. 'A cause of quarrel' is the twin *apple of discord*.
practice.shortcut: Apple of EYE = love; apple of DISCORD = quarrel.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A hot potato
options: a sensitive issue that people avoid dealing with
practice.solution: A hot potato is too hot to hold, so everyone passes it on. *A hot potato* = **a touchy issue nobody wants to handle**. 'A very easy task' is the food twin *a piece of cake*.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.

Taking sand to the Thar Desert to sell is like ___.
practice.solution: Newcastle was famous for coal, so taking coal there is pointless. The desert already has endless sand → **carrying coals to Newcastle** = taking something to a place that already has plenty.
practice.shortcut: Place already full of the thing → coals to Newcastle.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.

The quarrel over the window seat was just ___; the two friends were laughing together five minutes later.
practice.solution: A big fuss over a small matter that ends quickly = **a storm in a teacup**.
practice.shortcut: Big fuss + tiny cause = storm in a teacup.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.

The day Priya received her appointment letter was ___ for the whole family.
practice.solution: A joyful, memorable day = **a red-letter day** (special days were marked in red on calendars). The others do not describe a day.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To leave no stone unturned
options: to be careless in one's work
practice.solution: Turning every stone = searching everywhere. *Leave no stone unturned* = **make every possible effort**. 'Careless' is the opposite.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Under the weather
practice.solution: *Under the weather* = feeling a little unwell. The storm option is literal.
practice.shortcut: Health family: under the weather = not well.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To turn the tables
options: to cheat in a game of cards
to reverse a situation and gain the upper hand over an opponent
practice.solution: *Turn the tables* = to change a losing position into a winning one against someone. 'Lose badly' is the opposite; furniture is literal.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A fair-weather friend
options: a loyal friend in all situations
a friend who stays only in good times
practice.solution: Fair weather = good times. A *fair-weather friend* disappears when trouble comes. 'A loyal friend' is the opposite.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A snake in the grass
options: a hidden enemy who pretends to be a friend
practice.solution: A snake hidden in grass strikes without warning. *A snake in the grass* = **a treacherous person who hides behind friendship**.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

A man of straw
options: a person with a strong will
a person of no real importance or strength
practice.solution: Straw is light and weak. *A man of straw* = a weak person with no real substance or power. 'Scarecrow' is literal; 'strong will' is the opposite.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.

Tired of ___ to his elder brother in the family business, Karan started his own shop.
practice.solution: Karan was unhappy with a lower role → **playing second fiddle** (taking a less important position). The others mean winning, being satisfied with past success, and running away.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.

Seeing the police van, the pickpocket ___.
practice.solution: A thief who sees the police runs away → **took to his heels** (ran away fast).

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To bell the cat
options: to take a great risk for the good of others
to tie a bell on a pet
practice.solution: In the fable, the mice wanted a bell on the cat but nobody dared to tie it. *Bell the cat* = **to face the danger that others fear, for everyone's benefit**.
practice.shortcut: Fable of the mice → the brave, risky job.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given phrase.

A Herculean task
options: a task that is very easy
a task that needs very great effort
an order given by a king
practice.solution: Hercules, the hero of Greek stories, did twelve extremely hard labours. *A Herculean task* = **a job needing enormous strength or effort**.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To open Pandora's box
options: to start something that causes many unexpected problems
to open a box of gifts
practice.solution: In the Greek story, Pandora opened a forbidden box and let all kinds of troubles into the world. *Open Pandora's box* = **start something that leads to many new problems**.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate word to complete the idiom.

Rahul does not believe in hiding the truth; he always calls a spade a ___.
practice.solution: The fixed idiom is *call a spade a spade* = to speak plainly and honestly. Idioms are frozen: 'a spade a shovel' is not the idiom.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate word to complete the idiom.

The new supervisor likes to have a finger in every ___.
practice.solution: The fixed idiom is *have a finger in every pie* = to be involved in (or meddle in) many matters.
practice.shortcut: Recall the frozen chain: finger → every pie.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate word to complete the idiom.

Don't count your chickens before they ___; the result is not out yet.
practice.solution: The fixed idiom is *don't count your chickens before they hatch* = don't depend on a gain before it is certain.

practice.q:
Select the idiom that can replace the words in bold.

The two neighbours have been **openly and bitterly hostile to each other** for years.
practice.solution: *At daggers drawn* = in open, bitter enmity. *At sixes and sevens* = in confusion; *on cloud nine* = very happy; *at a loose end* = having nothing to do.

practice.q:
Select the option that can replace the words in bold.

Priya **always speaks plainly, without softening her words**.
practice.solution: *Not mince matters (or words)* = to speak frankly without softening. *Beat about the bush* is the opposite; *sit on the fence* = avoid taking sides; *pull one's weight* = do one's fair share of work.
practice.shortcut: Mince = cut small = soften; never mince = speak plainly.

practice.q:
Select the idiom that can replace the words in bold.

In the final debate, Aman's argument **won and was accepted by everyone**.
practice.solution: *Carry the day* = to win or be successful. *Fall flat* = fail to have the intended effect; *miss the bus* = lose an opportunity; *go to the dogs* = be ruined.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To have the upper hand
options: to raise one's hand to ask
to be in a weak position
to have control or an advantage
practice.solution: Upper = above the other. *Have the upper hand* = to be in control or in a stronger position. 'Weak position' is the opposite.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

At sixes and sevens
practice.solution: *At sixes and sevens* = in a state of confusion or disorder. The number options are literal; 'perfect order' is the opposite.
practice.shortcut: Numbers in an idiom are never literal.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To go to the dogs
options: to be ruined or become much worse
to go for a morning walk
practice.solution: *Go to the dogs* = to decline badly or be ruined (a business, a person, a place). 'Improve greatly' is the opposite.

practice.q:
Select the option that is OPPOSITE in meaning to the given idiom.

To keep one's chin up
practice.solution: *Keep one's chin up* = stay brave and cheerful in hard times. Its opposite is **to lose heart**. 'Stay cheerful' is the same meaning (the trap).
practice.shortcut: Write the meaning (stay brave), then reverse it.

practice.q:
Select the option that is OPPOSITE in meaning to the given idiom.

To blow hot and cold
options: to hold the same opinion firmly
practice.solution: *Blow hot and cold* = to keep changing one's mind, to be unsteady. Opposite: **to hold one opinion firmly**. 'Keep changing one's opinion' is the same meaning.
practice.shortcut: Hot then cold = changing; opposite = steady.

practice.q:
Select the option that is OPPOSITE in meaning to the given idiom.

To be in someone's good books
options: to be out of favour with someone
practice.solution: *Be in someone's good books* = to be in their favour. Opposite: **out of favour** with them. 'Liked by someone' repeats the meaning.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given phrase.

To call off
practice.solution: *Call off* = cancel: *The match was called off because of rain.* The phone and shouting options use the plain verb *call*.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given phrase.

To put up with
practice.solution: *Put up with* = to bear or tolerate something unpleasant: *I cannot put up with this noise.*

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given phrase.

To look down upon
practice.solution: *Look down upon* = to think that someone is less important than oneself. 'Respect' is the opposite; 'from a height' is literal.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

We have run ___ of sugar; please buy some on your way home.
practice.solution: *Run out of* = to have no more left. Only *out* forms this phrase with *of*.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Our car broke ___ on the highway, so we had to wait for a mechanic.
practice.solution: A machine that stops working *breaks down*. *Break out* is for war, fire or disease; *break up* ends a relationship; *break in* is forced entry.

practice.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The police have promised to look ___ the complaint and find out the truth.
practice.solution: *Look into* = to investigate. 'Find out the truth' confirms investigation.

practice.q: Select the phrasal verb that means *to stop a habit*.
practice.solution: *Give up* smoking = stop the habit. *Give in* = surrender; *give out* = distribute or stop working; *give away* = donate or reveal.

practice.q: Select the phrasal verb that means *to refuse an offer or request*.
practice.solution: *Turn down* an offer = refuse it. *Turn up* = arrive; *turn out* = prove to be; *turn over* = flip, or hand over.

practice.q: Select the phrasal verb that means *to look or behave like an older family member*.
practice.solution: *She takes after her mother* = she resembles her mother. *Take off* = remove or leave the ground; *take up* = start a hobby or job; *take in* = deceive or absorb.

practice.q:
Select the phrasal verb that can replace the word in bold.

The fire brigade managed to **extinguish** the fire within an hour.
practice.solution: *Put out* a fire = extinguish it. *Put off* = postpone; *put on* = wear or switch on; *put up* = raise or stay.

practice.q:
Select the phrasal verb that can replace the words in bold.

My grandfather **recovered from** his illness quickly.
practice.solution: *Get over* an illness = recover from it. *Get through* = pass or finish; *get along* = be friendly with; *get off* = leave a bus or escape punishment.

practice.q:
Select the phrasal verb that can replace the words in bold.

Ramesh **happened to meet** an old school friend at the railway station.
practice.solution: *Come across* = meet or find by chance. *Come about* = happen; *come off* = succeed or become detached; *come out* = appear or be published.
